title: Influencer convicted of helping Abby Choi’s ex-husband flee; former father-in-law recounts day of killing
text:
Influencer convicted of helping Abby Choi’s ex-husband flee; former father-in-law recounts day of killing | Lianhe Zaobao 
 Singapore International China Business Opinion Lifestyle Entertainment Search Published / 21 Nov 2026 15:55 S M L XL Influencer convicted of helping Abby Choi’s ex-husband flee; former father-in-law recounts day of killing
 AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here. 
 Influencer Pun Hau-yin was convicted of conspiracy to pervert the course of justice and sentenced to six months in prison for helping Alex Kwong, the ex-husband of murder victim Abby Choi (left), attempt to flee. （From Abby Choi’s and Pun Hau-yin’s Instagram accounts） (Hong Kong) As the trial over the 2023 killing and dismemberment of Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi continues, influencer Pun Hau-yin has been convicted of conspiracy to pervert the course of justice and sentenced to six months in prison for helping Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong, attempt to flee. 
 Pun appealed against her conviction and sentence. Her barrister argued that a friend known as “Ivy” had misled her into believing Kwong was a legitimate businessman rather than a wanted man. The barrister also sought a reduced sentence on the grounds that her involvement was limited. The judge dismissed both appeals in a written ruling. Pun, who had been granted bail pending appeal, must now begin serving her six-month sentence immediately. 
 Birthday celebrations and hairy crab before prison 
 Pun faced one count of conspiracy to pervert the course of justice. The charge alleged that between 24 and 25 February 2023, knowing that Alex Kwong might face an investigation, she conspired with a woman known as “Ivy” to commit an act tending and intended to pervert the course of justice: helping Kwong leave Hong Kong urgently and secretly outside official, lawful channels. 
 Despite her legal troubles, Pun has continued to post photographs on social media of meals and outings with friends, including birthday celebrations. She also wrote: “I hope heaven sees the truth. Heaven is watching what people do. Looking forward to it.” In her “last moments of freedom” before entering prison, she shared photographs of a hairy crab meal in the early hours. 
 In a further development in Choi’s case on 18 November, her former father-in-law, 69-year-old defendant Kwong Kau, gave evidence in his own defence at Hong Kong’s High Court. He became emotional and wept as he recalled receiving a call from his elder son, Anthony Kwong, on the day of the killing. He admitted in court that he had dismembered Choi’s body after her death, but insisted that he had never planned to kill her. He also maintained that neither of his sons had been involved in dismembering her body. 
 Kwong Kau recounted the events of 21 February 2023, the day of the killing. He said he drove to Hong Kong’s Lung Mei Village sometime after 11am, then drove to Tai Mei Tuk, where he parked and exercised. At about 3pm, he received an unexpected call from Anthony Kwong. According to Kwong Kau, his son told him that something very serious had happened and that Choi appeared to have lost consciousness. His other son, Choi’s ex-husband Alex Kwong, was crying at the time. 
 Three defendants admit only to preventing lawful burial 
 Kwong Kau suddenly broke down in tears in the witness box while describing the call, briefly interrupting proceedings. The judge asked whether he needed a break, but he declined and continued giving evidence. When the hearing turned to the dismemberment of Choi’s body after her death, Kwong Kau admitted under questioning by his lawyer that he had carried it out. 
 Despite admitting to dismembering Choi’s body, Kwong Kau maintained in court that he had never planned to kill her. He also denied that anyone else had planned the killing in advance. 
 Choi was killed in February 2023. Her former husband Alex Kwong, 32, his elder brother Anthony Kwong, 35, and their father Kwong Kau were charged with murdering her in Hong Kong on 21 February 2023, and preventing the lawful burial of her body between 21 and 23 February that year. 
 All three defendants deny murder but have pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of a body. Kwong Kau’s claims that he alone dismembered the body and that his sons were not involved remain part of his defence. The court has yet to determine their criminal responsibility on the evidence.
